prompt: On a target machine with 64-byte cache lines, an array traversal benchmarks faster than traversing a linked list whose nodes are scattered across the heap. Both sum the same n integers in Θ(n) time (time proportional to n). What explains a possible gap?

options.text: The array has contiguous access and spatial locality; the list follows dependent pointers that may miss in cache
options.explanation: Correct. The next node address depends on loading the current node. This serial dependency and poor spatial locality can make scattered traversal slower; exact latency requires target-specific measurement.

options.text: Linked lists are Θ(n log n) to traverse because of pointer overhead
options.explanation: Traversal is still Θ(n), proportional to the number of nodes n: one step per node. The difference is in the constant factor per step, not the growth rate. Here n is the input item count.

options.text: The compiler can't optimise linked list code at all
options.explanation: Compilers can optimise both. The dependent memory accesses in the specified scattered list remain a possible bottleneck; the claim that no optimisation is possible is too strong.

options.text: Linked lists store more data, so there's more to add up
options.explanation: The values added are the same. The extra pointer per node increases memory traffic a bit, but the main cost is latency from scattered, dependent accesses.

workedExample: A contiguous array lets nearby accesses reuse cache lines. Scattered list traversal also depends on loading each next pointer before knowing the following address. Both visit n values, so both are linear, but the cost per visit can differ. Measure the target workload; the explanation does not establish a universal speed ratio.

options.text: B, because it accesses columns, which are stored contiguously in C
options.explanation: C multidimensional arrays store complete rows consecutively; the column direction is not contiguous.

options.text: Neither: both are Θ(N^2) and do the same additions
options.explanation: The loops have the same Θ(N^2) work and arithmetic but different access patterns; N is side length. Asymptotic growth does not capture locality.

options.text: A walks adjacent entries; B jumps by a full row stride
options.explanation: Correct. The column index selects adjacent elements within a row. Changing row while holding column fixed jumps across rows.

options.text: A, because it has fewer loop iterations
options.explanation: Both visit every cell exactly once. The difference is the cost of memory accesses.

workedExample: In row-major storage, changing the column within one row reaches adjacent elements. Changing the row while holding the column fixed jumps by a full row stride. Both loops visit the same number of cells, but A has better sequential locality. Cache reuse across later columns depends on cache capacity and associativity, so measure the speed difference.

prompt: Consider a natural merge sort on n items that uses binary insertion sort to extend short runs to a bounded target of at most 64 elements. Why can this quadratic subroutine fit an O(n log n) overall sort?

options.text: Because insertion sort is Θ(n) on every input
options.explanation: The worst-case moving cost is still quadratic in run length. Binary search reduces position-finding comparisons, not the number of elements that may need to shift.

options.text: Because insertion sort uses less memory than merge sort for large n
options.explanation: It's true insertion sort is in place, but that's not why it's used here. It's chosen for speed on small pieces.

options.text: To guarantee stability, which merge sort can't provide
options.explanation: Merge sort is stable, and so is Timsort's merge step. Stability isn't the reason.

options.text: A fixed cap bounds the small-run cost, so total extension work stays linear
options.explanation: Correct. The bounded run length caps the quadratic subroutine at a fixed cost; distributing such runs across the item count gives linear total extension work. Small-run constants make it worthwhile.

workedExample: The short-run cap is a fixed constant, independent of total input length n. Quadratic work on each capped run is bounded by a constant times that run’s length. Summed across all runs, extension work is linear; the merge stage can retain O(n log n) overall time. The cap and practical crossover are implementation choices.

prompt: A colleague proposes replacing a tuned matrix-multiplication implementation with another that has a smaller asymptotic exponent. What is the best response before adopting it for your workload?

options.text: Keep the existing baseline until representative benchmarks show that the proposed implementation is faster and meets memory and accuracy needs
options.explanation: Correct. A smaller exponent alone does not establish performance for a particular matrix workload. Constants, implementation, memory and numerical behaviour matter.

options.text: Adopt it immediately because its exponent is smaller
options.explanation: A smaller exponent does not quantify finite-size time without constants, implementation and workload details.

options.text: Adopt it only for square matrices, since the exponent only applies to them
options.explanation: Input shape matters for benchmarking, but squareness alone does not establish a performance benefit.

options.text: Use Strassen's algorithm instead, since it is always faster than Θ(n^3)
options.explanation: Strassen is not universally faster. Its extra work, memory use and numerical behaviour require evaluation for the target workload.

workedExample: A smaller exponent describes eventual growth under a cost model, not performance at the stated finite size. Require an actual implementation and benchmark representative shapes and numeric types. Compare peak memory and numerical accuracy as well as elapsed time. Keep the existing measured baseline until the alternative demonstrates the needed improvement.

prompt: Which factors can explain why a Θ(n²) algorithm beats a Θ(n log n) algorithm over a particular finite input range? Here n is the input size, log denotes its base-2 logarithm. Select all that apply. Let A be Θ(n log n) and B be Θ(n²).

options.text: Inputs are always tiny, say at most 30 items
options.explanation: Yes. Below the crossover point the asymptotic class doesn't decide anything; a simple quadratic loop with tiny constants often wins. This is why sorting libraries use insertion sort for small pieces.

options.text: A chases pointers through scattered heap nodes, while B scans a contiguous array
options.explanation: Yes. Dependent cache misses can inflate A’s measured cost per operation. Exact latency depends on hardware and workload.

options.text: A's constant factor is hundreds of times larger than B's
options.explanation: Yes. A much larger coefficient can let the faster-growing quadratic model win over a finite range. Measure the range relevant to the workload.

options.text: Larger n alone guarantees that the quadratic algorithm wins
options.explanation: False. Slower asymptotic growth wins eventually, but no finite crossover is implied without constants.

options.text: Both are written in the same programming language
options.explanation: A shared language does not by itself favour either implementation. Their operations and representations can still differ.

workedExample: Finite-range performance includes constants, allocation and access patterns. Small inputs, expensive dependent memory accesses in A, or a much larger coefficient in A can let B win. Larger input alone eventually favours A’s slower growth under fixed comparable cost models. Sharing a language does not determine the winner.
